title: I have, I don't have, I need
intro: One verb opens up a whole world of conversation: dāshtan, 'to have'. In this lesson you learn all its forms, how to say you do not have something, how to ask how many of something someone has, and how to say what you need – at home, in a shop and at a friend's house with a very curious cat.
goals: say what you have and do not have with dāshtan
ask 'do you have…?' and 'how many … do you have?'
say what you need with lāzem dāshtan
use chand-tā and yek for counting things

sections.title: Tom visits Amir
sections.context: Tom, an Australian student in Tehran, visits his classmate Amir at home for the first time. A cat walks in.

lines.en: Amir, do you have a cat?

lines.fa: بله، دو تا گربه دارم. این پیشی است، آن یکی ملوس.
lines.r: bale, do tā gorbe dāram. in Pishi ast, ān yeki Malus.
lines.en: Yes, I have two cats. This one is Pishi, that one is Malus.
lines.faV: بَله، دو تا گُربه دارَم. این پیشی اَست، آن یِکی مَلوس.

lines.fa: چه قشنگ! من در خانه حیوان ندارم.
lines.r: che ghashang! man dar khāne heyvān na-dāram.
lines.en: How pretty! I don't have an animal at home.
lines.faV: چه قَشَنگ! مَن دَر خانه حَیوان نَدارَم.

lines.en: You don't have a dog either?

lines.fa: نه، سگ هم ندارم. اما در استرالیا خانواده‌ام یک سگ دارد.
lines.r: na, sag ham na-dāram. ammā dar Ostorāliyā khānevāde-am yek sag dārad.
lines.en: No, I don't have a dog either. But in Australia my family has a dog.
lines.col: نه، سگ هم ندارم. اما تو استرالیا خانواده‌م یه سگ داره.
lines.colR: na, sag ham na-dāram. ammā tu Ostorāliyā khānevāde-m ye sag dāre.
lines.faV: نه، سَگ هَم نَدارَم. اَمّا دَر اُستُرالیا خانِواده‌اَم یِک سَگ دارَد.
lines.colV: نه، سَگ هَم نَدارَم. اَمّا تو اُستُرالیا خانِواده‌م یه سَگ داره.

lines.fa: چای می‌خوری؟ قند داریم، شکر هم داریم.
lines.r: chāy mi-khori? ghand dārim, shekar ham dārim.
lines.en: Will you have tea? We have sugar cubes, and we have sugar too.
lines.faV: چای می‌خوری؟ قَند داریم، شِکَر هَم داریم.

lines.en: Yes, thanks. Do you have milk too?

lines.fa: متأسفانه شیر نداریم. گربه‌ها همه‌ی شیر را خوردند!
lines.r: mota'assefāne shir na-dārim. gorbe-hā hame-ye shir rā khordand!
lines.en: Unfortunately we don't have milk. The cats drank all the milk!
lines.col: متأسفانه شیر نداریم. گربه‌ها همه‌ی شیر رو خوردن!
lines.colR: mota'assefāne shir na-dārim. gorbe-hā hame-ye shir ro khordan!
lines.faV: مُتَأَسِّفانه شیر نَداریم. گُربه‌ها هَمه‌یِ شیر را خوردَند!
lines.colV: مُتَأَسِّفانه شیر نَداریم. گُربه‌ها هَمه‌یِ شیر رو خوردَن!

lines.fa: مهم نیست. من چای را بدون شیر دوست دارم.
lines.r: mohem nist. man chāy rā bedun-e shir dust dāram.
lines.en: It doesn't matter. I like tea without milk.
lines.faV: مُهِم نیست. مَن چای را بِدونِ شیر دوست دارَم.

lines.en: Do you have a brother or a sister?

lines.fa: یک خواهر دارم. اسمش امیلی است. چند تا عکس از او دارم. می‌خواهی ببینی؟
lines.r: yek khāhar dāram. esm-ash Emili ast. chand tā aks az u dāram. mi-khāhi bebini?
lines.en: I have one sister. Her name is Emily. I have a few photos of her. Do you want to see?
lines.faV: یِک خواهَر دارَم. اِسمَش اِمیلی اَست. چَند تا عَکس اَز او دارَم. می‌خواهی بِبینی؟

sections.title: The most useful verb after 'to be'
sections.md:
[[داشتن|dāshtan|to have]] is the second verb every learner needs. Iranians use it for far more than owning things: you *have* a sister, *have* time, *have* a cold, *have* twenty years (that is how you say your age – remember lesson 4), and you *have* love for something: [[دوست داشتن|dust dāshtan|to like, to love]] is literally *to have (as) a friend*.

It is also one of the few verbs whose present tense has **no mi-** in front. Compare [[می‌روم|mi-ravam|I go]] with [[دارم|dāram|I have]]. The endings are the same ones you already know from *khub-am, khub-i, khub-ast…*

To say you do **not** have something, put [[نَـ|na-]] in front: [[ندارم|na-dāram|I don't have]]. The stress jumps onto *na-*: NA-dāram.

items.note: present stem dār-; no mi- in the present
a pet cat is often called پیشی pishi
Iranians drink tea with a lump of ghand, not stirred-in sugar
one word, two meanings – and also 'tap'!

ex.en: How many sisters do you have?

sections.title: dāshtan – all six forms
sections.md: The stem is **dār-**; add the personal endings. There is no *mi-*. For the negative add **na-** to the front.

examples.en: He / she doesn't have a bicycle.

sections.title: Counting things: yek, chand tā and the singular
sections.md:
After a number the noun stays **singular**: [[دو گربه|do gorbe|two cats]], never *do gorbe-hā*. In everyday speech Iranians slip the little counting word [[تا|tā]] between the number and the noun: [[دو تا گربه|do tā gorbe]]. It is optional, but it makes you sound natural.

To ask *how many?* use [[چند تا|chand tā]] (or just [[چند|chand]] before a noun). The same words mean *a few* in a statement: [[چند تا عکس دارم|chand tā aks dāram|I have a few photos]].

For *one / a*, use [[یک|yek]] before the noun, or the little ending [[ـی|-i]] you met in lesson 3: [[یک خواهر دارم|yek khāhar dāram]] = [[خواهری دارم|khāhar-i dāram]]. When the thing is not counted at all – milk, money, time – the bare noun is enough: [[پول ندارم|pul na-dāram|I have no money]].

examples.en: How many brothers do you have?
How many Persian books do you have?

examples.note: yeki = 'one (of them)' when the noun is not repeated.

sections.title: Saying what you need
sections.md:
[[لازم داشتن|lāzem dāshtan|to need]] works exactly like *dāshtan*; the word [[لازم|lāzem|necessary]] sits right before the verb: [[من چتر لازم دارم|man chatr lāzem dāram|I need an umbrella]]. The thing you need comes before *lāzem*.

A second way, very common in speech, is impersonal: [[چتر لازم است|chatr lāzem ast|an umbrella is necessary]] – no subject at all.

examples.fa: امروز هوا بد است. چتر لازم داریم.
examples.r: emruz havā bad ast. chatr lāzem dārim.
examples.en: The weather is bad today. We need an umbrella.
examples.faV: اِمروز هَوا بَد اَست. چَتر لازِم داریم.

examples.fa: برای این کتاب عینک لازم دارم.
examples.r: barā-ye in ketāb eynak lāzem dāram.
examples.en: I need glasses for this book.
examples.faV: بَرایِ این کِتاب عَینَک لازِم دارَم.

examples.note: hich chiz 'nothing' goes with a negative verb – two negatives are normal in Persian.

sections.title: Mina's bag
sections.intro: Mina is leaving for university and checks her bag. Read, then answer the questions.

sentences.fa: مینا هر روز یک کیف بزرگ دارد.
sentences.r: Minā har ruz yek kif-e bozorg dārad.
sentences.en: Mina has a big bag every day.
sentences.faV: مینا هَر روز یِک کیفِ بُزُرگ دارَد.

sentences.fa: در کیفش سه تا کتاب و دو تا دفتر دارد.
sentences.r: dar kif-ash se tā ketāb o do tā daftar dārad.
sentences.en: In her bag she has three books and two notebooks.
sentences.faV: دَر کیفَش سه تا کِتاب و دو تا دَفتَر دارَد.

sentences.fa: یک موبایل و یک عینک هم دارد.
sentences.r: yek mobāyl o yek eynak ham dārad.
sentences.en: She also has a mobile phone and a pair of glasses.
sentences.faV: یِک موبایل و یِک عَینَک هَم دارَد.

sentences.en: But today she doesn't have her key!
The key is on the kitchen table.

sentences.fa: مینا وقت ندارد. مادرش کلید را به او می‌دهد.
sentences.r: Minā vaght na-dārad. mādar-ash kelid rā be u mi-dahad.
sentences.en: Mina has no time. Her mother gives her the key.
sentences.faV: مینا وَقت نَدارَد. مادَرَش کِلید را به او می‌دَهَد.

questions.q: How many books does Mina have in her bag?
What does she not have today?

sections.title: Cats, tea and sugar cubes
sections.md:
The long-haired **Persian cat** – [[گربه‌ی ایرانی|gorbe-ye irāni]] – is one of the world's oldest breeds, and street cats are everywhere in Iranian cities; many families leave food out for them. Dogs are less common as pets in cities, so *sag dāri?* is a rarer question than *gorbe dāri?*

Offering tea is the first thing a host does, and the answer to *chāy mi-khori?* is almost always yes. Tea comes in small glasses with a bowl of [[قند|ghand|sugar cubes]]: you put the cube in your mouth and sip the tea through it, rather than stirring sugar in. Milk in tea is a foreign habit – which is why Amir's house had none.

sections.title: Tips
items: The stress in a negative verb moves to the front: **NA**-dāram, **NA**-dāri. Hearing where the stress falls tells you at once whether the answer is yes or no.
**shir** means both 'milk' and 'lion' – and a tap. Context does all the work: *shir dāram* in a kitchen is about milk.
Persians count with the singular: *panj ketāb* 'five books', *dah nafar* 'ten people'. The plural **-hā** is only for uncounted groups: *ketāb-hā* 'the books'.
*dust dāram* is 'I like' and 'I love' at once. For a person it means love; for tea it means like. Lesson 10 uses it for food.

items.q: We have a car. → ما یک ماشین ___
Which sentence means 'She doesn't have a dog'?

items.q: How do you ask a friend 'How many sisters do you have?'
items.explain: chand tā asks 'how many'; dāri is the 'you (friend)' form.

items.q: Which is correct Persian for 'two cats'?
